q1.questionText: API latency is variable & app is sluggish. How do you design UI safely?

whatWorkedWell: Clearly identified the problem as a network reliability issue rather than a UI rendering issue
Proposed optimistic UI updates with rollback — a production-grade pattern
Mentioned skeleton screens and shimmer loaders to handle perceived performance
Correctly brought up retry logic with exponential backoff for failed requests
overallTakeaways: Strengthen your answer by quantifying thresholds — e.g. 'show skeleton after 300ms, error state after 5s'
Consider mentioning offline-first architecture and local caching strategies like React Query or SWR
Next time, structure your answer: Problem → Approach → Trade-offs → Monitoring

keyMoments.description: Strong opening — immediately framed the problem around user perception, not raw latency
Mentioned optimistic UI updates with a concrete example of a payment confirmation flow
Hesitated when asked about error boundary strategies — could have been more specific
Correctly identified that skeleton screens reduce perceived load time by up to 40%
Did not mention request cancellation or debouncing for rapid user interactions
Wrapped up well by connecting the solution back to business impact — fewer drop-offs

q2.questionText: Design a distributed rate limiter that works across multiple data centers.

whatWorkedWell: Correctly identified Token Bucket and Sliding Window as viable algorithms
Mentioned Redis as a centralized counter store — a real-world production choice
Brought up the challenge of clock synchronization across data centers
Discussed graceful degradation when the rate limiter itself is unavailable
overallTakeaways: Dive deeper into consistency vs availability trade-offs for distributed counters
Mention sticky sessions or local + global rate limiting as a hybrid approach
Quantify — e.g. '1000 req/s per user, 50K req/s globally' to show practical thinking

keyMoments.description: Immediately clarified scope — per-user vs per-API vs global rate limiting
Drew a clear comparison between Token Bucket and Leaky Bucket algorithms
Missed the opportunity to discuss race conditions in distributed counter increments
Proposed a Redis Lua script for atomic increment — excellent production insight
Did not address how to handle rate limit headers in HTTP responses
Strong finish — discussed monitoring dashboards to track rate limit violations

Discussed CDN caching for popular queries as a scaling strategy
Brought up personalization using user search history
overallTakeaways: Consider discussing the data pipeline — how search logs are aggregated and fed back into the Trie
Mention sharding strategies for the Trie across multiple servers
Talk about debouncing on the client side to reduce unnecessary backend calls

keyMoments.description: Started with requirements clarification — latency target under 100ms
Explained Trie traversal clearly with a whiteboard-style walkthrough
Overlooked the challenge of handling typos and fuzzy matching in autocomplete
Proposed a two-tier caching strategy — in-memory LRU and distributed Redis cache
Did not discuss A/B testing for ranking algorithm improvements

whatWorkedWell: Proposed a queue-based architecture to handle traffic spikes gracefully
Mentioned inventory pre-allocation with distributed locks to prevent overselling
Discussed CDN and static asset optimization to reduce origin server load
Brought up database read replicas and caching layers
overallTakeaways: Address the virtual waiting room pattern — used by Flipkart during Big Billion Days
Discuss circuit breakers and bulkheads to isolate checkout from other services
Mention load testing strategies — how would you simulate 10M concurrent users?

keyMoments.description: Framed the problem well — distinguished between read-heavy browsing and write-heavy checkout
Proposed message queues (Kafka/SQS) for async order processing — production-grade
Was vague about how to handle payment failures and rollback inventory reservation
Mentioned Redis-based distributed locks for inventory — correct approach
Did not discuss idempotency for payment retries — a critical oversight
